cards.front: A {{c1::pathogen}} is a microbe or virus that causes disease in its host.
cards.quote: A pathogen is a microbe or virus that causes disease in its host.

cards.front: What is a strain of a microbe, and why does it matter for whether the microbe helps or harms?
cards.back: A strain is a genetic variety within one kind of microbe. Whether a microbe helps, harms or does neither can depend on its strain and on where it lives.
cards.quote: Whether a microbe helps, harms or does neither can depend on its strain (a genetic variety within one kind of microbe) and where it lives.

cards.front: Name four ways pathogens can harm a host.
cards.back: By blocking, by damaging tissue, by releasing poisons called toxins, or by setting off harmful responses in the host.
cards.quote: Pathogens harm in several ways: by blocking, by damaging tissue, by releasing poisons called toxins, or by setting off harmful responses in the host.

cards.front: In nitrogen fixation, what does the word "fix" mean?
cards.back: Fix means fasten, not repair: fastening nitrogen into a compound that cells can build with.
cards.quote: To fix nitrogen is to fasten it into a compound that cells can build with (fix as in fasten, not repair).

cards.front: Which living things can fix nitrogen, and what else fixes it besides life?
cards.back: Only some bacteria and archaea can. Lightning and fertilizer factories fix nitrogen too.
cards.quote: Among living things, only some bacteria and archaea, a second group of single-celled microbes, can do it; lightning and fertilizer factories fix nitrogen too.

cards.front: Nodule bacteria in legumes join nitrogen to hydrogen to make {{c1::ammonium}}, which the plant builds into its proteins and DNA.
cards.quote: The nodule bacteria in soybeans, peanuts and other legumes join nitrogen to hydrogen to make ammonium

cards.front: A student splits a soybean nodule and finds it pink inside. What can the student conclude about nitrogen fixing, and what can the student not conclude?
cards.back: Pink is a good clue that bacteria are fixing nitrogen, but it is not proof, and it says nothing about how much is fixed.
cards.why: The amount has to be measured another way, such as the nitrogen isotope comparison in the field data.
cards.quote: Pink or red is a field sign of fixing: a good clue, not proof, and silent on how much.

cards.front: A farmer harvests soybeans and carries the beans away. Does any of the nitrogen the nodule bacteria fixed stay in the field? Explain.
cards.back: Some does. Most fixed nitrogen ends up in the beans, but the roots, stems and leaves that die in the field are broken down by decomposers, and some fixed nitrogen returns to the soil.
cards.quote: When the rest of the plant dies, decomposers break down its roots, stems and leaves, and some fixed nitrogen returns to the soil

cards.front: Where does a decomposer do its digesting, and what does the work?
cards.back: Outside the microbe, on the dead matter itself. Enzymes the microbe releases do the work.
cards.quote: They break down wastes as well as dead organisms, and the digesting happens outside the microbe, on the dead matter itself, where the released enzymes work.

cards.front: In a model ecosystem, you switch off all the decomposers. What happens to dead leaves and the nutrients in them?
cards.back: Dead matter piles up with its nutrients locked inside, so the nutrients are not available to plants.
cards.quote: Without them, dead matter would pile up with its nutrients locked inside.

cards.front: In an Ohio stream study of fallen maple and oak leaves, which grew more, fungi or bacteria?
cards.back: Both grew on the leaves, and the fungi always outweighed the bacteria.
cards.quote: in an Ohio stream study, both fungi and bacteria grew on fallen maple and oak leaves, and the fungi always outweighed the bacteria.

cards.front: A {{c1::microbiome}} is the community of microbes that live in one place, such as soil, a stream or a body.
cards.quote: the community of microbes that live in one place, such as soil, a stream or a body.

cards.front: Your body cannot digest fiber, yet fiber can still give you energy. How?
cards.back: Gut bacteria in the large intestine ferment fiber into small acids, and the cells lining the large intestine can use those acids as a source of energy.
cards.quote: The cells lining the large intestine can use the small acids the bacteria make as a source of energy.

cards.front: In a 2016 study, mice with human gut bacteria ate a low-fiber diet. What did their gut bacteria begin to do?
cards.back: They began feeding on the protective mucus that lines the gut.
cards.quote: mice carrying a set of human gut bacteria and fed a low-fiber diet had gut bacteria that began feeding on the protective mucus that lines the gut.

cards.front: How does yogurt form from milk?
cards.back: Two kinds of bacteria ferment the sugar in milk and release lactic acid, which thickens the milk and makes it sour.
cards.quote: Yogurt forms when two kinds of bacteria ferment the sugar in milk and release lactic acid, which thickens the milk and makes it sour.

cards.front: How can E. coli be used to make human insulin?
cards.back: E. coli carrying lab-made genes for human insulin makes insulin's two parts, and researchers join the parts into human insulin.
cards.quote: E. coli carrying lab-made genes for human insulin made its two parts, which researchers joined into human insulin

cards.front: How does the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa harm a grapevine?
cards.back: It causes Pierce's disease, which blocks the vine's water-carrying tubes.
cards.quote: causes Pierce's disease, which blocks the vine's water-carrying tubes

cards.front: Most E. coli live quietly in the large intestine, yet some people get sick from E. coli in food or water. What explains the difference?
cards.back: Some strains carry extra genes that make them harmful. Swallowing enough of those strains can make a person sick.
cards.quote: some strains carry extra genes that make them harmful, and people who swallow enough of them in food or water can get sick

cards.front: A student claims, "E. coli is a germ, so it is harmful." Use the lesson's two factors to judge the claim.
cards.back: The claim is too broad. Strain matters: most strains live quietly in the large intestine, and some carry harmful genes. Place matters: gut E. coli that reaches the urinary tract is the most common cause of bladder infections.
cards.quote: Place matters too: E. coli from your own gut is the most common cause of bladder infections, which start when it reaches the urinary tract

cards.front: By one widely cited estimate, about what share of the ocean's microbial biomass do viruses kill each day, and how firm is that number?
cards.back: Roughly a fifth. The estimate is rough and varies a lot from place to place.
cards.quote: By one widely cited estimate, viruses kill roughly a fifth of the ocean's microbial biomass (the total mass of its microbes) every day.
cards.section: Explain: viruses and diseases reshape ecosystems

cards.front: In a lab model ecosystem, a virus killed the ocean alga Phaeocystis and bacteria broke down the dead cells. What did the water gain?
cards.back: About 148 micrograms of nitrogen and 7 micrograms of phosphorus per liter that other living things could use.
cards.quote: After bacteria broke down the dead algae, the water gained about 148 micrograms of nitrogen and 7 micrograms of phosphorus per liter that other living things could use.

cards.front: In seawater, one kind of bacterium becomes far more common than the others. Will its phages spread faster or slower than phages of rare bacteria, and what follows for the rare kinds?
cards.back: Usually faster. A phage spreads when an infected cell bursts and its new phages meet the next host, and a common host is easier to meet. The common kind can be cut back hardest, which may leave room for rarer kinds.
cards.why: It does not always happen: some bacteria resist their phages, and some phages hide inside cells.
cards.quote: A phage spreads when an infected cell bursts and its new phages meet the next host, and a common host is easier to meet.
cards.section: Explain: viruses and diseases reshape ecosystems

cards.front: In a 2019 coastal water experiment, viruses switched from hiding inside bacteria to bursting them. What happened to the bacterial community, and which idea from the lesson explains it?
cards.back: The bacterial community became more diverse. This is consistent with kill the winner: cutting back common hosts may leave room for rarer kinds.
cards.quote: A 2019 experiment on coastal water found that when viruses switched from hiding to bursting, the bacterial community became more diverse.

cards.front: In 2006 at the Michigan field trial, nodulating soybeans held 282 kg N/ha above ground and non-nodulating soybeans held 150 kg N/ha. How much more did the nodulating plants hold, as a percentage of the non-nodulating value?
cards.back: Difference: 282 - 150 = 132 kg N/ha. Percentage: 132 / 150 x 100 = 88 percent more.
cards.quote: Write it as a percentage of the non-nodulating value (divide the difference by the non-nodulating value, then multiply by 100).
cards.section: Elaborate: how much nitrogen do nodules add?

cards.front: In the Michigan trial, nitrogen from fixation in nodulating soybeans was 195, 95.0 and 90.3 kg N/ha in 2006, 2007 and 2008. What was the mean over the three years?
cards.quote: Find the mean nitrogen from fixation over the three years.
cards.section: Elaborate: how much nitrogen do nodules add?

cards.front: In 2007 nodulating soybeans held 144 kg N/ha above ground, of which 95.0 came from fixation. What percent came from fixation, and does that fit the lesson's stated range?
cards.back: 95.0 / 144 x 100 is about 66 percent. It fits: each year fixation supplied about 61 to 69 percent of the above-ground nitrogen.
cards.quote: Each year the bacteria supplied about three-fifths to two-thirds of the nodulating plants' above-ground nitrogen (61 to 69 percent).
cards.section: Elaborate: how much nitrogen do nodules add?

cards.front: In 2006 nodulating soybeans held 282 kg N/ha and fixed 195, but they beat non-nodulating plants (150) by only 132. Explain the mismatch.
cards.back: Nodulating plants got only 87 kg N/ha (282 - 195) from other sources such as soil, versus 150 for non-nodulating plants. With a partner supplying nitrogen, they took less from other sources, so the gap is 63 kg N/ha smaller than the fixation estimate.
cards.quote: With a partner supplying nitrogen, the nodulating plants got less from those other sources, so the 132 gap is 63 kg N/ha smaller than the isotope estimate.
cards.section: Elaborate: how much nitrogen do nodules add?

cards.front: In a test of nodule bacteria on soybeans, why should the pots use sterile, nitrogen-poor potting mix?
cards.back: Ordinary soil may already hold nodule bacteria, which would put bacteria into the control group.
cards.quote: Sterile mix matters, because ordinary soil may already hold nodule bacteria.

cards.front: In a test of nodule bacteria on soybeans, name the independent variable, the control and two dependent variables you could measure.
cards.back: Independent variable: bacteria added or not added. Control: pots of the same sterile, nitrogen-poor mix with no inoculant. Dependent variables: dry plant mass after six weeks, nodules per plant, or how many split nodules are pink.
cards.quote: Control: pots of the same sterile, nitrogen-poor potting mix with no inoculant.

cards.front: In a 10-pot-per-group soybean test, the inoculated and uninoculated plants end with the same mean mass. What should you check, and what can you not conclude?
cards.back: Check the roots: the bacteria may not have formed nodules. You cannot conclude the bacteria do not help soybeans, because the test may not have worked.
cards.quote: If both groups match, the bacteria may not have formed nodules, so check the roots.
